questions.q: Which population profile is given for SLE on the opening page?
questions.exp: SLE is described as a disease of women of reproductive age (20–40) with 9:1 female predominance. (Book p452)

questions.q: What concordance is cited for identical twins in SLE?
questions.exp: The source lists positive concordance in >40% of identical twins and strong family history. (Book p452)

questions.q: What lupus-nephritis frequency contrast is shown?
questions.exp: Lupus nephritis is shown in adults 50–60% and childhood SLE 100%. (Book p452)

questions.q: An elderly person develops new postmenopausal SLE. Which clinical profile is favoured in the source?
opts: Good prognosis with no CNS/renal symptoms and sicca/serositis/musculoskeletal symptoms
Severe nephritis with low complement in every case
questions.exp: Postmenopausal SLE has good prognosis, no CNS/renal symptoms, sicca/serositis/musculoskeletal symptoms, anti-Ro positive, anti-dsDNA negative and normal complements. (Book p452)

questions.q: Which statement is made about prognosis and active-serology in SLE?
opts: Active SLE has anti-Ro only with normal complement
Male SLE has poor prognosis; active SLE has anti-dsDNA positivity and low complement
Male SLE has better prognosis and high C3
questions.exp: The bottom notes state male SLE has poor prognosis; active SLE markers are anti-dsDNA positive and low complements. (Book p452)

questions.q: What defective-clearance substrates initiate the printed SLE pathogenesis pathway?
questions.exp: Genetic/environmental causes lead to defective clearance of apoptotic and NETotic debris, triggering immune dysregulation. (Book p453)

questions.q: Which innate receptors are explicitly shown in the SLE pathogenesis diagram?
questions.exp: TLR-7 and TLR-9 are labelled pattern-recognition receptors; hydroxychloroquine is drawn inhibiting this step. (Book p453)

questions.q: What is called the central key pathogenic cytokine in SLE?
questions.exp: Activated plasmacytoid dendritic cells produce type I interferon/IFNα, identified as the central key pathogenic cytokine; anifrolumab is shown blocking it. (Book p453)

questions.q: Which helper-T-cell balance is drawn in SLE?
opts: Treg greater than all helper cells
Th2 greater than Th17 with Th1 also shown
questions.exp: The diagram depicts Th1, Th2 > Th17; Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 aid B-cell activation. (Book p453)

questions.q: Which ligand/cytokine is marked upregulated in SLE and promotes B-cell stimulation?
questions.exp: BAFF/B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) is shown upregulated in SLE; belimumab inhibits it. (Book p453)

questions.q: Immune-complex deposition in which three sites is depicted as type-III hypersensitivity?
questions.exp: B cells form immune complexes/type-III hypersensitivity that deposit in glomerulus (GN), synovial cavity (synovitis) and vessels (vasculitis). (Book p453)

questions.q: Which HLA alleles are listed as genetic factors for SLE?
questions.exp: HLA factors listed: HLA-DR3 (seen in subacute cutaneous lupus) and HLA-DR2. (Book p454)

questions.q: What is the strongest complement-deficiency risk factor ranking printed for SLE?
opts: C1q deficiency greater than C2 deficiency greater than C4 deficiency
C4 deficiency greater than C2 greater than C1q
questions.exp: Early complement deficiency affects debris clearance; ranking is C1q > C2 > C4 deficiency. (Book p454)

questions.q: Which chromosome/gene association is explicitly given?
questions.exp: Non-HLA factors include increased X-chromosome number → increased risk/IRAK gene, and chromosome 3 → TREX gene. (Book p454)

questions.q: Which environmental exposure is listed as an autoimmune trigger through stimulation of pulmonary alveolar macrophages?
questions.exp: Environmental factors include OCP, HRT, UV-B, EBV, silicosis (stimulates pulmonary alveolar macrophage → autoimmune trigger), vitamin-D deficiency and smoking. (Book p454)

questions.q: Which factor is labelled as having only minimal association in the source?
questions.exp: A bracket labels vitamin-D deficiency and smoking as minimal association; the source separately lists OCP, HRT, UV-B, EBV and silicosis. (Book p454)

questions.q: Which hormonal exposures are listed among SLE environmental factors?
opts: Oral contraceptive pills and hormone replacement therapy
questions.exp: OCP and HRT head the environmental-factor list. (Book p454)

questions.q: Which drug is shown blocking TLR-7/TLR-9 in the SLE pathogenesis illustration?
questions.exp: HCQ is drawn over TLR-7/TLR-9; belimumab targets BLyS and anifrolumab blocks type-I interferon signalling in the diagram. (Book p454)

units.title: 1. SLE Profile & Clinical Phenotypes
units.guide:
The epidemiologic profile introduces renal burden and age/sex prognostic groups.
Postmenopausal, male and active-SLE features are distinguished.
Pathogenesis begins with failed debris clearance and type-I interferon.

units.title: 2. Genetic & Environmental Etiology
units.guide:
HLA and non-HLA genetic risks are ordered before environment.
Complement deficiency is tied to failed debris clearance.
The source’s weak/minimal environmental associations are preserved rather than overstated.
